need this shaped into a formal RFC request for the database engineering work, with the decisions and operational steps easy to follow. please keep the production problem, schema audit, migration approach, safeguards, app changes, staging checks, and rollout window together in one coherent plan. This is for a zero-downtime index migration on our core PostgreSQL database, not a request to run anything now. The primary customer transactions ledger table gets severe lock contention during peak settlement windows. Analytical ingestion jobs and payment processing workers doing bulk ledger reconciliations trigger full sequential scans over transaction date intervals that do not have the needed index coverage. Storage volume read IOPS hit hardware saturation, CPU rises across the primary database nodes, and p99 checkout latency goes from 40 milliseconds to 3.5 seconds. The database engineering group needs a workflow that creates high-cardinality composite B-tree indexes without interrupting active application reads or writes. Use migration.sql and schema.prisma in the plan.

For the audit part, explain what is already present and what is missing. The transactions table has separate single-column indexes on customer_id and created_at, but no composite index covering merchant_account_id, status, and settlement_date. pg_stat_statements and the slow query plans show that analytical billing aggregations spend 82 percent of query duration evaluating bitmap heap scans with heavy filter rechecks. If we use ordinary DDL for the required indexes, it takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE table lock and blocks payment-worker INSERT and UPDATE traffic for 25 to 40 minutes. That is why a non-blocking strategy is needed. Please make the risk understandable without making it sound like the indexes are already built.

The intended approach is PostgreSQL CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on the multi-terabyte production tables. Mention that concurrent index creation takes two sequential table scans instead of one and avoids exclusive table locks while application writers keep changing records during the build. The migration runner has to use autocommit mode in migration.sql; these concurrent index builds cannot be run inside an explicit multi-statement transaction block. Set lock_timeout to 2 seconds and statement_timeout to 0 so the initial index declaration does not sit indefinitely waiting behind long-running analytical queries. Keep those settings distinct and explain their purpose.

There is failure cleanup to include as well. A concurrent build can fail if it hits a deadlock, a unique constraint violation, or a client disconnects before the second scan finishes. PostgreSQL terminates the process but can leave an invalid index catalog entry marked INVALID in pg_class. Those invalid indexes use disk, need ongoing write-ahead log maintenance when the table is written, and are not used by the query optimizer. The automation in migrate.ts needs to query pg_index and detect existing invalid index tokens before it starts new builds. When it finds one, run DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS before retrying creation so automated CD pipeline retries are idempotent. Keep the failure cases and the cleanup order clear.

Also cover the downstream replicas rather than treating the primary as the only concern. Production reads go to four physical streaming read replicas, with synchronous commit disabled. Index builds on the primary produce substantial write-ahead log volume that flows over the streaming links. If replica replay lag goes above 150 megabytes, replica queries may fail with “query canceled due to conflict” errors. monitor.py should continuously sample replay lag from pg_stat_replication. At more than 75 megabytes of replica byte lag, it should insert a 15-second throttling sleep between index build stages so the replicas can drain their WAL queues. Keep the 75 MB throttle point separate from the 150 MB level at which query failures may occur.

After the indexes are built and verified, include the application integration work, not just the DDL. Engineers need to change repository queries in transaction_repo.ts so where-clause criteria line up left to right with the index column order: merchant_account_id first, status second, then the settlement_date range. Update schema.prisma with the new @@index declaration and run prisma generate to refresh TypeScript query-client type signatures. Do not use destructive push migrations against production databases. The schema declaration, generated client, and repository query changes belong after index build completion and verification.

Before production, the reliability group has to check performance in staging restored from yesterday’s production volume snapshot. load_runner.ts should use k6 synthetic load generators to simulate 8,000 concurrent checkout transactions per second. Run the migration runner during the simulated traffic peak and verify median transaction response latency stays below 50 milliseconds, with zero deadlocks or transaction aborts logged across application connection pools. Keep these as staging validation criteria rather than claiming that they have already passed.

The planned production execution is Wednesday evening in the low-volume window from 02:00 to 03:00 UTC. The on-call database administrator will establish a live terminal session, check that background vacuum workers and scheduled backup snapshots are paused, and launch with the verified runner script. The incident coordinator should stay in active voice communication with platform engineering leads and track table bloat and CPU temperature across database cluster nodes until index build validation passes all integrity checks and query latencies stabilize at target baselines. Please organize all this into a formal RFC prompt with useful headings, preserving the details and making clear what needs to be prepared, monitored, and verified.

Our distributed real-time media communications network needs an exhaustive architectural evaluation. The review should cover ICE candidate gathering protocols, STUN server binding sequences, and relay media routing edges across native and web application clients. It needs to look at how these parts work across enterprise network configurations, including symmetric network address translation, restrictive corporate proxy firewalls, and carrier-grade NAT cellular gateways. With those configurations, media negotiation setup latencies frequently exceed four point two seconds. That delay is a serious concern for call setup, especially when clients are on mobile cellular connections or behind enterprise network boundaries.

In the worst-case network topologies, peer session negotiation experiences fatal connection establishment failures when dual-stack IPv4 and IPv6 candidate pairs do not resolve within the available timeout budgets. The audit should examine these failures alongside the setup delays, rather than considering candidate gathering by itself. The scope also includes client signaling state machines, protocol message serialization, edge relay allocation topologies, and end-to-end telemetry observability across the media pipeline. These are all parts of the same technical audit, and the review should assess the complete path from gathering and signaling through relay routing and telemetry.

2. Browser Peer Connection Lifecycle and Workspace File Tagging
Within the client signaling workers, developers need to inspect peer connection lifecycle state machines. Tag peer connection dot ts for the review of RTCPeerConnection configuration parameters. In particular, iceTransportPolicy needs to be set to all, and bundlePolicy needs to be set to max-bundle. The audit should check those settings in the client routines and not leave either parameter unspecified.

Client routines also need event handlers attached to onicecandidate and oniceconnectionstatechange. These handlers capture transient transitions in network interfaces, which matter as clients move between network conditions. The spoken tag cues need to map correctly to workspace references and their target files during code reviews. During rapid reconnect cycles, peer connection teardown routines must release audio track buffers and clean up WebGL video sink pipelines. They must do that without leaking browser memory allocations. Review the lifecycle and cleanup behavior as part of the same client-side inspection.

3. Session Description Protocol and Candidate Serialization Routines
The protocol encoding logic in session description dot rs needs to conform strictly to RFC 8445. Tag session description dot rs to inspect candidate attribute parsing for host, server reflexive, and relay candidate types. The parser has to validate candidate priority calculation formulas, check foundation token uniqueness, and validate component identification integers. IPv6 address representations must not be truncated during parsing or serialization.

The serialization harness also needs to validate candidate transport types in a controlled way. It should distinguish UDP from TCP active and TCP passive modes, rather than treating them as interchangeable. At the same time, malformed candidate attributes received from legacy SIP gateway peers should be discarded. The audit should check both the validation and the handling of malformed attributes, while maintaining the required RFC 8445 conformance and preserving complete IPv6 address representations.

4. Distributed TURN Relay Infrastructure Configuration and Credentials
Edge relay instances in geographic regions terminate STUN and TURN allocations under high concurrency. Review turn config dot yaml in the deployment directory for the authentication mechanisms, shared secret generation, and ephemeral credential lifetimes. All three parts of the configuration need to be examined as part of the relay infrastructure review.

The TURN configuration must enforce allocation bandwidth quotas of two megabits per second per stream. It must also set UDP buffer sizes to sixteen megabytes, to prevent packet loss during burst video keyframe transmissions. These values apply to the allocation and buffer requirements and should be checked in the configuration. Traffic should be balanced across diverse regional clusters using geographic DNS Anycast routing. That routing must preserve session stickiness while media calls are active; balancing regional traffic should not remove the required affinity for an active session.

5. Gathering State Machine and Trickle ICE Signaling Optimizations
Traditional WebRTC implementations wait for ICE candidate gathering to finish before exchanging SDP offer-answer envelopes. That ordering introduces unacceptable call setup latency over mobile cellular connections. The signaling gateway in gateway dot ts needs to implement Trickle ICE fully, so gathering does not have to finish before the initial offer is transmitted.

Client endpoints should send initial SDP offers immediately following host candidate discovery. They should then stream subsequent reflexive and relay candidates asynchronously across WebSocket signaling channels. The gateway and the client signaling behavior need to support this sequence. The signaling layer must also use exponential backoff retry schedules for candidate transmission acknowledgments. Those retries are intended to ensure that transient network disconnects do not abort ongoing call negotiations. The review should consider the initial offer timing, subsequent candidate delivery, and acknowledgment retries together.

6. Network Interface Switching, Multi-Homing, and Connection Migration
Mobile client applications frequently move between cellular radio data and local wireless networks during active voice calls. The media transport coordinator in transport dot rs must support ICE restart sequences and connection migration for these transitions. The requirement applies while calls are active, not just when establishing a new connection.

When client telemetry detects consecutive packet loss exceeding twenty percent, the engine must trigger an ICE restart. It must do so without tearing down the underlying media capture pipeline and without renegotiating audio codecs. The transport layer should also maintain background probing on dormant candidate pairs. That probing should enable zero-interruption failover during physical Wi-Fi disconnections. The audit needs to cover the loss condition, the restart behavior, the preserved capture and codec state, and background probing for the dormant pairs.

For enterprise compatibility, the media proxy layer must support TURN over TLS on port four hundred forty-three. The review should verify each of these requirements for the enterprise traversal path.

Media payload encryption must strictly enforce DTLS-SRTP key exchanges. The security boundary must also enforce certificate thumbprint pinning during peer negotiation. In addition, it must apply strict rate-limiting to unauthenticated STUN binding requests to mitigate distributed denial of service vectors. These encryption, peer negotiation, and request-limiting controls are all part of the security review, alongside TURN over TLS and the certificate and TLS settings.

8. Telemetry Dashboard, Quality of Experience Metrics, and Audit Sign-Off
Platform site reliability engineers must instrument Prometheus metrics for mean gathering duration, ICE failure ratios, and relay fallback percentages. These metrics should provide visibility into gathering performance, failures, and relay use across the media pipeline. The telemetry monitoring system must also establish automated alerts for regional edge aggregates when median round-trip times exceed one hundred fifty milliseconds or audio packet jitter exceeds thirty milliseconds.
